title: How to Fix MongoDB Duplicate Key Error E11000
subtitle: A complete guide to understanding why MongoDB throws E11000, what unique indexes actually do, and every way to fix this error depending on your situation.
content:
How to Fix MongoDB Duplicate Key Error E11000

You are building something. Everything is going fine. Then suddenly your terminal or browser throws this at you:

MongoServerError: E11000 duplicate key error collection: mydb.users index: email_1 dup key: { email: "test@gmail.com" }

And you stare at it for a second thinking — wait, I did not do anything wrong. The code looks fine. So what is MongoDB actually complaining about?

This error is one of the most common things you will hit when working with MongoDB, especially with Mongoose. The good news is once you understand what is actually happening, fixing it becomes straightforward. Let me walk you through the whole thing properly.

What E11000 Actually Means

MongoDB throws E11000 when you try to insert or update a document that would create a duplicate value in a field that has a unique index on it.

A unique index is MongoDB's way of enforcing that no two documents in a collection can have the same value for a specific field. Think of it like a constraint. If your users collection has a unique index on the email field, MongoDB will flat out refuse to save a second user with the same email address. It does not matter if the rest of the document is completely different. Same email means rejected.

The error message itself tells you exactly what happened if you read it carefully:

E11000 duplicate key error collection: mydb.users index: email_1 dup key: { email: "test@gmail.com" }

Breaking this down: collection: mydb.users tells you which collection the conflict happened in. index: email_1 tells you which index was violated — the _1 suffix means it is an ascending index on the email field. dup key: { email: "test@gmail.com" } tells you the exact value that already exists in the database.

So the database is not broken. Your code is not broken. MongoDB is doing exactly what you told it to do — protecting the uniqueness of that field.
